entities.name: John of the Grating
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
John of the Grating (Jean de la Grille), a Cistercian monk, served as Bishop of Aleth in the Duchy of Brittany from 1144 until his death in 1168. His episcopate is singularly defined by his decisive action to relocate the ancient episcopal see from the vulnerable, exposed promontory of Aleth (modern Saint-Servan) to a more defensible, fortified island site that would become Saint-Malo. This strategic move, undertaken in 1146, was a pivotal moment in the ecclesiastical and urban development of Brittany, fundamentally reshaping the religious and economic geography of the region by establishing a new, resilient center.

The core of Bishop John's tenure was dedicated to this monumental transfer. Facing persistent threats from seaborne raiders, likely Norman or Viking remnants, who frequently harassed the exposed settlement of Aleth, John secured the necessary papal and ducal approvals to abandon the old cathedral of Saint-Pierre. He then initiated the construction of a new cathedral, dedicated to Saint Vincent, on the rocky island of Saint-Malo, just across the Rance estuary. This ambitious project involved not only the physical relocation of ecclesiastical administration but also the transfer of relics and the establishment of new fortifications, demonstrating a practical approach to episcopal governance in a turbulent era.

The relocation under John of the Grating had profound and lasting consequences. It catalyzed the growth of Saint-Malo from a small insular settlement into a formidable walled city and a major port, renowned for its maritime prowess and strategic importance for centuries. Conversely, Aleth gradually declined, eventually becoming Saint-Servan, a suburb of the very city that supplanted it. John's decision thus laid the groundwork for Saint-Malo's future as a powerful ecclesiastical and commercial hub, a testament to his foresight in safeguarding the church's stability and influence amidst regional instability.
